extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, reporters, and newspaper editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and an analytic outline for evaluating and producing newspaper news stories, covering news values, sourcing, structure, literary and typographical style, and special‑case guidance for fire/accident reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Values
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of questions to determine the newsworthiness and context of a story: In what paper was the story published? What are the policy and the character of the paper? How widely does the paper circulate outside of the place in which it is published? Does the paper appeal to a particular class of readers? Is the piece of news presented from the point of view of this class? What, for the average reader, is the source of interest in the news contained in the story? How much would the news interest the average reader? Why? Do you think that the news was worth more or less space than was given to it? Why? What more significant phases might have been played up or developed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider paper policy, audience, geographic reach, source of reader interest, proportionality of space, and possible undeveloped significant phases. Evaluate relative news value to determine prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of News
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about origin and verification of the news: How did the news originate? Where was the first record of it probably made? By whom? What records and what persons may have been consulted in securing the news? What reference books or material may have been used in getting or in verifying the details of the story? What other possible sources might have been consulted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze provenance, primary records, interviewed persons, documentary/reference checks, and possible additional sources omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of News Gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate evidence of reporting methods: What evidence does the story give of the methods by which the news was obtained? Is there any evidence that the reporter or correspondent failed to get any of the important details of the piece of news?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs of firsthand reporting, interviews, document use, and omissions indicating failures to gather important details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose (fairness and impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess fairness and social effect: Does the story seem to be fair and unbiased? Is there evidence that any important facts were suppressed or that the story was colored to conform to the policy of the paper? Is the handling of the news constructive or destructive in its effect? What, if any, is the constructive purpose of the writer? Is the story so treated as to tempt the reader to imitate anti-social acts?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge bias, suppression, alignment with paper policy, and whether treatment encourages constructive outcomes or harmful imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of Story (form and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the story's primary purpose and form: Is the primary purpose of the story to inform or to entertain? Is the story largely narrative and descriptive? Is it largely explanatory? Is it largely direct or indirect quotation? If narrative, is the order chronological? Is the narrative clear or confused? Does the narrative move slowly or briskly? Are accounts of the event by participants or eye-witnesses used, and are they direct or indirect quotations? Are remarks and conversation of participants and eye-witnesses given? Is the description detailed or suggestive and effective? Is there a striving for effect in the description? If the story is that of a speech, report, etc., is the material arranged in logical order? Is much or little made of the personal, or human interest, element in the story of the speech or the interview?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify story type (informative/feature/human interest), narrative order, clarity, pacing, use and form of witness accounts, descriptive depth, and presence of human-interest angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the Story (lead, body, arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about overall structure: Has the story a summary lead or an unconventional beginning? Does the lead contain the essential facts concisely presented? Is the most striking detail played up as the feature in the first group of words of the opening sentence of the lead? What other element in the news might have been featured in the lead? Is the lead proportionate in length to the whole story? How are the details arranged in the body of the story? Is there any evidence that the story was cut down in making up the paper? Are the paragraphs closely connected? Is there unnecessary repetition in the story? Could the arrangement of the details be improved? How?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate lead type and effectiveness, proportionality, body arrangement, evidence of cuts, paragraph connectivity, repetition, and opportunities to improve ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphs (literary style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze paragraph-level construction: What is the average length of the paragraphs? Are any of the paragraphs too long or too short? Is each paragraph a unit? Are the details well arranged and closely connected in the paragraphs? Does the first group of words at the beginning of each paragraph attract the reader as his eye glances down the story? Could any of the paragraph beginnings be made more effective? Also: Because of the narrowness of the columns the newspaper paragraph must be comparatively short to avoid appearing heavy and uninviting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check unity of topic in each paragraph, coherence within, effective paragraph openings to attract the eye, and appropriateness of paragraph length for newspaper columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence construction (literary style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze sentence-level construction: What is the average length of the sentences? Are any of the sentences too long or too short? Is the construction of each sentence evident in rapid reading? Is each sentence a unified expression of a closely related group of ideas? Are the parts of the sentences combined in firm, closely knit construction? Do the sentence beginnings attract the reader by the importance and the interest of the ideas expressed in the first group of words? Do any of the sentences trail off loosely into a succession of phrases and clauses? Is there variety in sentence length and sentence construction?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sentence unity, clarity in rapid reading, tight syntax, engaging openings, avoidance of trailing phrases, and variety to maintain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate word choice and diction: Is the style concise or wordy? Is the diction original or hackneyed? Is the style marked by many adjectives or by superlatives? Are the verbs specific and forcible? Is the diction too learned for the comprehension of the average rapid reader? Are words used idiomatically and accurately? Are slang and colloquial expressions found in the story, and what is the effect of them? Is the diction keeping with the tone of the story? Specific words in original combinations are always preferable to colorless, general terms and trite phrases. Technical, scientific, and learned words should be avoided unless fully explained. Slang and colloquial expressions may be used when the tone of the story justifies them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific, original diction and forcible verbs; avoid overly learned vocabulary without explanation; use slang/colloquial only if tone justifies; watch adjectives and superlatives to prevent hackneyed style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of style (overall readability and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess qualities such as clearness, force, animation, humor, pathos, and taste: Can the details of the story be easily comprehended in rapid reading; that is, is the style comparatively simple? Upon what does the general clearness of the story depend? Is the movement slow or rapid? Why? Is there any humor or pathos in the story? How is the humorous or the pathetic effect secured? Has the news possibilities for humorous or pathetic treatment that are not developed? Is the story in good taste?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge overall readability in rapid scanning, pace, emotional effects (humor/pathos), how they are achieved, and whether the treatment maintains good taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph length guideline (newspaper vs ordinary prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric guideline for newspaper paragraphs: The typical newspaper paragraph contains from 35 to 75 words, whereas the average paragraph in ordinary prose is from 150 to 250 words in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for comparatively short paragraphs (35–75 words) in newspaper copy to avoid heavy, uninviting appearance in narrow columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of involved constructions and long periodic sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Involved constructions, long periodic sentences, and similar rhetorical devices have no place in journalistic writing, because they tend to prevent rapid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor direct, rapid‑reading sentence constructions; avoid ornate rhetorical forms that slow comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis by initial position
rubrics_metrics.description: The emphasis given to an important point by placing it at the beginning of a sentence or a paragraph is a distinctive characteristic of newspaper style, growing out of the fact that in rapid reading the eye catches important points quickly if they occupy these initial positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place important points early in sentences/paragraphs to ensure they are noticed during rapid reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe typographical peculiarities and consistency: Peculiarities in such details of typographical style as abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, and the use of numerical figures should be noted in each story and associated with the newspaper from which the story was taken, for each paper has a typographical style of its own. One style is as good as another, but it is essential that consistency be maintained. The printing of significant facts in a box at the beginning or in the body of a story, often in bold-face type, the method of arranging lists of dead and injured, the forms for market reports, scores in sports, and similar details should be carefully noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and follow the paper's established rules for abbreviations, capitalization, hyphenation, numerals, boxed facts, lists, and other typographical devices; maintain internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fires and Accidents — Type of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for classifying fire and accident reports: Many newspaper reports of fires and accidents may be considered as typical examples of narrative and descriptive news stories of the purely informative type. The essential facts of the news are presented in a simple, direct, concise manner without any attempt to give the story any greater interest for the reader than the facts themselves possess. When human life is involved, writers may add personal or human-interest elements while presenting facts fully and accurately. Less important incidents may be treated as features if they lend themselves to human-interest, humorous, or pathetic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to keep report strictly informative or develop human-interest/feature elements; ensure facts remain full and accurate when adding human elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fires and Accidents — Purpose (constructive vs sensational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the social effect and constructive potential: Stories of fires and accidents, particularly when fatalities occur, may be written to be either constructive or destructive in their influence. The constructive effect lies in emphasis upon elements that (1) warn the reader's attention to preventive measures, (2) create sympathy for the victims, or (3) inspire admiration for heroism or other virtues. Stories that give prominence to immediate or underlying causes and responsibility as well as possible preventive measures have a helpful effect. Stories that aim to satisfy readers' interest in ghastly and sensational phases pander to morbid curiosity and have an unwholesome influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer emphasis on causes, responsibility, and prevention; avoid sensationalism that panders to morbid curiosity even if facts are true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fires and Accidents — Treatment of material
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended narrative/treatment techniques: All types of fire and accident stories give opportunity for spirited narrative and vivid description. Possible means for lending life and interest to the narrative include accounts of the disaster, either in direct or indirect quotation form, as secured by interviews with survivors and eye-witnesses, and conversation between persons involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid descriptive detail and eyewitness/interview material (direct or indirect quotes) to enliven narrative while preserving accuracy and constructive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fires and Accidents — Contents of story (essential details)
rubrics_metrics.description: List of important details to include and consider in analyzing unexpected-occurrence stories: (1) number of lives lost; (2) number of lives endangered; (3) names of dead and injured; (4) prominent persons and places involved; (5) character and extent of damage; (6) property threatened with damage or destruction; (7) cause and responsibility; (8) investigations; (9) preventive measures against recurrence of event; (10) probable or actual effects; (11) peculiar and unusual circumstances; (12) humorous and pathetic incidents. Almost any one of these details may be the feature of the story, and as such may be played up in the lead. The space and prominence given to each of these details are determined by its relative news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coverage of these items as appropriate, choose which detail to feature in the lead based on relative news value, and allocate space/prominence accordingly.
